newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails House vote in favor of MFN for China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails House vote in favor of MFN for China.

text.p: President Bill Clinton praised the House of Representatives vote on Tuesday maintaining normal U.S. trade relations with China as a top White House official called the annual review "corrosive."
The House, in a vote of 259 to 173, rejected a measure that would have overturned Clinton's decision to extend for one year Most Favored Nation (MFN) trade status with China.

"It sends a clear signal to our friends and foes alike that when it comes to America's security and prosperity, our nation speaks with one voice," Clinton said in a statement issued by the White House.
"Today's vote was a vote for America's interests," Clinton said. "It makes clear that the right way to encourage further progress in China is not to cut China off but to draw China in."
Samuel Berger, the White House national security adviser, said the final vote in what has become an annual test of wills over renewing MFN showed a wider winning margin than he had expected.
"I think what you see here...is an overriding appreciation and understanding and acceptance of the proposition that we can't ignore a quarter of the world's people," Berger said.

"If we want to cooperate with them, if we want to deal with them, to deal with the problems that we have with them, we are better to do that through engaging with them than through trying to tear this relationship apart," he said.
The margin was smaller than in the 286-to-141 vote last year supporting MFN renewal for China but still reflected sizable support for Clinton's policy.

Opposition this year was particularly vehement, in part because of concern about the fate of Hong Kong after the British colony returns to Chinese rule on July 1 and allegations that Beijing tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.
"There is a growing consensus behind ... a policy of engagement," Berger said when asked if the White House would favor making MFN status for China permanent.

"We'll have to consult with leaders of Congress over the weeks and months ahead to see whether we can get out from under this annual debate, which tends to be rather corrosive of the relationship," he said.
"This may be one of the most complex relationships in the world, the relationship between the United States and China," Berger said.

"Our point has not been that we don't have any problems with China," he said. "Our argument has been that the way to deal with those problems is not to isolate China or, even more specifically, isolate ourselves from China."
Berger called the annual review of MFN status "a clumsy instrument ... to force people into a box which says, 'I'm either voting for engagement or I'm voting for isolation.'"
